title: Legacy client embed proxy: streaming + rerank consistency playbook
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Problem: Legacy clients expect synchronous, page-based embeddings/rerank endpoints with stable cursor tokens and conventional HTTP error semantics. New runtime capabilities (streaming responses, function/tool calling hooks, and structured JSON outputs) improve latency and UX but break assumptions for those clients. We need a lightweight compatibility proxy + playbook that preserves observable correctness for legacy integrations while allowing newer clients to opt-in to streaming/structured/tool calls.

Goals:
- Guarantee idempotent, stable cursors for paged results even when underlying model responses are streamed or partially cached.
- Provide deterministic error mapping so legacy clients see well-scoped 4xx/5xx signals and get retry hints for safe retry/backoff.
- Support function/tool-call based rerank hooks without leaking streaming partials to clients that cannot handle them.
- Allow incremental rollout: opt-in headers for new behaviors, canary routing for a subset of customers, full migration path.

High-level approach:
1) Compatibility facade (proxy) sits in front of the raw inference API and exposes the classic embed/rerank HTTP iterator contract. The facade will: 
   - Convert streaming model outputs into a materialized page response for legacy clients by buffering until a page boundary or timeout.
   - Emit a stable cursor token computed from a deterministic snapshot (request fingerprint + last-seen-record-id + tombstone hash) so retries/duplicates are safe.
   - Translate structured output/toolcall signals into payloads that retain semantic parity: produce "toolcall_results" artifacts in the page response and mark when tool calls were invoked.

2) Error mapping: 
   - Map transient runtime errors (GPU OOM, kernel fail, 502/503) to 502 with "retry-after" and a "retryability": "transient" hint in our response JSON. 
   - Map user errors (invalid params, unsupported model-version, auth) to 4xx consistent with existing embed/rerank API shape. 
   - Surface a compact error-code namespace: EMB-PERM-400 (bad input), EMB-RATE-429 (rate limit), EMB-SERV-502 (transient), EMB-QUANT-422 (unsupported quantization for this request). Document mapping in compatibility guide.

3) Pagination semantics: 
   - Cursor design: 3-part base64 token: {version}.{snapshot_hash}.{offset_encoded}. The facade guarantees that snapshot_hash is stable for the life of a query snapshot; tombstone semantics will ensure removed documents are skipped but cursors remain valid.
   - Hybrid iterator: prefer streaming to deliver first-page quickly, but for legacy pages the facade will wait up to N ms (default 250ms) to assemble the first page. If streaming produces partial records, the proxy will only return complete records and mark the page as partial with a header X-Partial-Page: true when fewer-than-requested items are delivered due to timeouts.

4) Tool/function calling and structured outputs: 
   - For legacy clients, the proxy will materialize tool-call outputs into an array at result-level (tool_calls: [...]) and include a best-effort summary field (structured_summary) so clients that expect text/ranking scores continue to work. 
   - For clients that opt-in via Accept: application/x-redwood-structured+json or X-Redwood-Streaming: enabled, the facade will forward streaming chunks and the toolcall event stream with an event-type envelope.

Acceptance criteria / API contract examples: 
- GET /v1/embeddings/iterate?page_size=20&cursor=... returns { items: [...], next_cursor: "...", status: "partial|complete", error_hint: null } for success. 
- Error example: 502 { code: "EMB-SERV-502", message: "transient runtime failure", retryability: "transient", retry_after_seconds: 10 }
- Streaming opt-in: POST /v1/embeddings/stream with header X-Redwood-Streaming: enabled returns SSE multipart events: {event: "item", data: {...}} and an end event with final_cursor.

Migration and rollout plan:
- Implement facade feature-flagged behind "compat/embed-proxy". Start with internal customers and a small subset of integrations.
- Canary: route 5% of traffic for accounts with label "legacy-embed" and gather metrics for cursor stability, error-frequency delta, and latency.
- Add telemetry: record metrics for "compat.buffer_time_ms", "cursor_regeneration_rate", "toolcall_materialization_rate" and track by customer.
- Docs: publish migration guide and compatibility matrix in Confluence and include code samples for both legacy adapter and streaming client.

Testing and verification:
- Unit tests for cursor determinism (same snapshot + same offset -> same cursor).
- Integration tests with legacy clients: replay historical request traces and verify responses match previous contract within tolerance for ordering and content.
- Chaos tests: inject partial model streams and assert facade does not return corrupt/incomplete JSON.

Open decisions / trade-offs:
- Buffering latency vs. compatibility: 250ms timeout is a starting point; may increase for low-throughput models but must be configurable per-customer.
- Cursor size: we prefer base64 snapshot hash to avoid leaking internal IDs, but this requires a compact canonicalization function.
- Error namespace design: keep short codes to avoid long-term compatibility baggage but provide rich metadata for observability.

Related artifacts:
- Design doc: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/INF/Legacy+Embed+Proxy+Streaming+Compatibility
- Reference PR (prototype): https://github.com/redwood/inference/pull/12234
- Postmortem sample for cursor regressions: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1YX-example

Next steps:
- Product to sign off on buffering policy and customer opt-in header semantics (owner: Diego).
- Eng to prototype facade library and a lightweight in-proxy cursor encoder (owner: Jay Kim).
- Design to review the client-facing error table and sample payloads (owner: Sam Chen).
